raw_case_text:
A 65-year-old man was admitted to the hospital because of generalized weakness, coughing, and sputum production. Two months before his admission, weakness, sweating and anorexia had developed together with an intermittent cough and whitish sputum production. His slowly worsening symptoms brought him to the hospital.
The patient had eaten raw pork several times 20 years ago, but there was no specific family history.
Vital signs were as follows: Temperature 36 , pulse 98/min, and respiration 20/min. The blood pressure was 110/75 mmHg.
On examination the patient appeared weak and chronically ill. Although consciousness was clear, his general appearance and nutritional condition were not good. His conjunctiva and cornea appeared normal. His lungs were clear without crackles or wheezing. S1 was normal and S2 was normally split. No murmur was heard. An abdominal examination disclosed mild tenderness to deep palpation in the right upper quadrant, without diminution of bowel sounds; the liver was palpated by four finger breadths. Neurological examinations were negative. There were multiple subcutaneous nodules in the upper extremities and axillas.
Laboratory data on admission were as follows: Hemoglobin and hematocrit were 13.9 g/dl and 41.8% on admission; white cell count was 8700 with 4% eosinophils; urine and stool specimens gave normal results; blood urea nitrogen 5 mg/dl; creatinine 1.3 mg/dl; total protein 8.1 g/dl; albumin 4.3 g/dl; and SGOT/GPT 42/32 u/dl. HBsAg and HBsAb were negative.
The stain for acid fast bacilli and cytologic examination of sputum did not reveal anything microscopically.
The pulmonary function test was within normal range; the FEV1 was 4.1, the FEV1/FVC was 87%.
An X-ray film of the chest showed multiple nodular densities throughout both lower lung fields (Fig. 1). A computed tomographic scan of the brain and chest revealed multiple nodular and small calcified densities (Fig. 3, 4).
A biopsy of a subcutaneous nodule was done on the 4th hospital day, and upon microscopic examination, a bladder worm (Fig. 5):its hooks (Fig. 6) and parenchymatous portion with spinal canal and separated bladder of the cysticercus (Fig. 7):was observed. On the 12 th hospital day, the presence of cysticercus was confirmed by an open lung biopsy (Fig. 8).
Afterward, the patient was treated with praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day for 15 days and discharged on the 18 th hospital day, even though he still reported some weakness, cough, and sputum production. One month after discharge, his symptoms began to improve. Six months after treatment, the subcutaneous nodules had decreased to half in size. An X-ray film of the chest revealed nearly normal conditions in the lungs(Fig. 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive generalized weakness, sweating, anorexia, intermittent cough, and whitish sputum production.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months prior to admission, the patient developed generalized weakness, diaphoresis, and anorexia accompanied by an intermittent cough productive of whitish sputum, all of which slowly worsened until hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: He had consumed raw pork several times 20 years earlier. Family history was unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for generalized weakness, sweating, anorexia, cough, and sputum production.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were temperature 36 °C, pulse 98/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and blood pressure 110/75 mmHg. He was alert and oriented but appeared weak, chronically ill, and poorly nourished. Lungs were clear, heart sounds were normal, and abdominal exam revealed mild right upper quadrant tenderness on deep palpation with hepatomegaly (liver palpable 4 fingerbreadths below the costal margin). Neurological examination was normal. Multiple subcutaneous nodules were palpable in the upper extremities and axillae.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, hematocrit 41.8%, WBC 8,700/mm3 with 4% eosinophils, BUN 5 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, total protein 8.1 g/dL, albumin 4.3 g/dL, SGOT/SGPT 42/32 U/dL, negative HBsAg and HBsAb, normal urinalysis and stool exams, and negative sputum acid-fast bacilli stain and cytology. Pulmonary function tests were normal (FEV1 4.1 L, FEV1/FVC 87%). Chest X-ray showed multiple nodular densities throughout both lower lung fields.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain and chest CT scans revealed multiple nodular and small calcified densities in the brain and lungs. Biopsy of a subcutaneous nodule on hospital day 4 and open lung biopsy on hospital day 12 microscopically demonstrated a cysticercus bladder worm with characteristic hooklets, spiral canal, parenchymatous portion, and bladder wall.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated cysticercosis involving the brain (neurocysticercosis), lungs, and subcutaneous tissues was histopathologically confirmed by subcutaneous nodule and open lung biopsies. He was treated with oral praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day for 15 days and discharged on hospital day 18. His symptoms began improving 1 month post-discharge, and at 6-month follow-up, his subcutaneous nodules had decreased by half in size and chest radiograph was nearly normal.
